title: A hard chapter
hookLine: the ancients, it says, kept people simple rather than clever, a line scholars read in very different ways (Tao Te Ching 65)

lines: A LINE THAT STOPS A READER.
WHAT IF YOU READ IT TWICE?
cards: Some lines in old books make a reader put the book down. Chapter sixty-five of the Tao Te Ching has one.
On a first reading, it sounds like advice for keeping people in the dark, written for rulers who'd like their subjects easy to manage. Some readers stop there, and that's a fair place to stop.
Others go back and read it again.

teach.b: First, what it says. In James Legge's translation, the ancients skilled in the Tao used it "not to enlighten the people, but rather to make them simple and ignorant."
People are hard to govern, the chapter goes on, when they know too much. Ruling a state by cleverness is a thief to the state; ruling without it is a blessing.

Second, the first reading. Taken at face value, that's a ruler's dream: keep the population uninformed, and it stays easy to manage. Some readers take the chapter exactly that way and are troubled by it.
That reaction deserves room; the text says what it says.
Third, the second reading. The Chinese word behind simple is the same word chapter twenty uses when the speaker calls their own heart the heart of a fool, while everyone else seems bright and sure.
With that in mind, some hear plain and unscheming rather than kept ignorant, and the target may be scheming cleverness, the kind that games every system.
Notice, too, who the chapter warns most sharply: the ruler who governs by cleverness. Fourth, why read it twice at all. The chapter doesn't settle which reading is right, and neither will today.
But a hard line read once tends to become a verdict; read twice, it becomes a question. That habit works well beyond old books: the email that stung, the headline, the comment from a parent.
The second reading doesn't always change the meaning. It changes how fast you decide.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching differ over chapter sixty-five: some read it as advice to keep people uninformed, others as praise of plainness over scheming, and some readers go through it slowly, more than once, to weigh both.

games.q: you meet a line in an old book that troubles you. what does today's lesson do with chapter sixty-five?
o: read it twice and hold both readings.
decide the book is simply wrong.
games.why: the lesson sets two readings side by side, control or plainness, and points out that chapter twenty uses the same word for the speaker's own heart.

practice: Hear the line once the way it first lands: the ancients did not make the people clever, but simple.
Notice what rises, suspicion maybe, or a shrug, then hear it again with simple meaning plain and unscheming, like the speaker's own fool's heart in chapter twenty.
You don't have to pick a winner; hold the two readings side by side, like two cups, one in each hand.

wordCard.voice: A hard chapter. Chapter sixty-five's line about keeping people simple, read in more than one way. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: simple, plain, foolish; chapter sixty-five uses it for the people, chapter twenty for the speaker's own heart.
